entry.title: Retracing the Final Days of Vincent Van Gogh | Sotheby’s

media:group.media:title: Retracing the Final Days of Vincent Van Gogh | Sotheby’s
media:group.media:description:
Walking through the streets that inspired one of Vincent van Gogh’s final masterpieces.
Here, Sotheby’s Simon Shaw visits Auvers-sur-Oise, the village outside of Paris where the artist spent the last months of his life. It is also where he painted ‘Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees),’ the star of Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection coming to Sotheby's New York.
Within days of arriving at Auvers in May 1890, Van Gogh chose the chestnut trees as one of his primary subjects. ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’ is the only example that includes figures––three women in bright dresses and a lone man who may represent the artist himself. Van Gogh sculpted the voluminosity of the mighty trees with intense, multi-layered brushwork of dabs and dashes. Extraordinary ranges of color exaggerate the natural hues of the foliage, surrounded a dark blue halo of the sky.
After over 50 years in private hands, ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’ will be on view at the Breuer starting 7 November before the auction on 18 November.

entry.title: 5 Things That Make A 1960 Kusama Infinity Net So Rare | Sotheby's

media:group.media:title: 5 Things That Make A 1960 Kusama Infinity Net So Rare | Sotheby's
media:group.media:description:
Yayoi Kusama's 1960 red Infinity Net, No. 3P.B., comes from the very start. She would go on making these works for more than 60 years.
The idea traces back to a red tablecloth in her mother's house, its pattern imagined expanding outward until it enveloped her. It continued on her flight from Japan to the United States, looking out at an infinite expanse of waves. Her early nets came mostly in white and red, and many of the reds lean toward orange. This one is pure red.
It was also the painting that first gave Kusama hope of breaking into a male-dominated, overwhelmingly white New York art world. Shown at the Whitney in 1961–62, it hung alongside many of the greatest American artists of her generation. Up close, its impasto rises into peaks — the same pull toward the infinite that would later fill her Infinity Rooms.
No. 3P.B. will be offered in The Now & Contemporary Evening Auction, presented by CELINE, at Sotheby's New York on 16 November.

entry.title: Experience the Paris that Renoir, Pissarro, Monet Lived In | Sotheby’s

media:group.media:title: Experience the Paris that Renoir, Pissarro, Monet Lived In | Sotheby’s
media:group.media:description:
Monet, Pissarro and Renoir: three Impressionist visions of 19th-century Paris. Claude Monet's Le Jardin des Tuileries is an urban view that is hardly urban at all. Three quarters of the picture is foliage and grass, the visual sensation of light and weather.
Camille Pissarro does the opposite. Haussmann and Napoleon III had knocked down medieval Paris and replaced it with the grand boulevards. By 1898, Pissarro had come to terms with this modernity. Painted from the Hôtel du Louvre, one of a series of 15, his view runs up the Avenue de l'Opéra to the Opéra itself, alive with horses and people.
At the weekend, the middle classes could escape the city. Argenteuil was 15 minutes away by train, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir's En canot, from the mid-1870s, puts you on the boat beside an almost life-size figure.
All three come from the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection, one of the finest collections remaining in private hands today. They will be offered at Sotheby's New York on 18 November in Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection Evening Auction.

media:group.media:title: The Earliest Karuizawa 1960s Ever Bottled | Sotheby's
media:group.media:description:
Following the sale of a legendary Karuizawa 1960 in New York, Sotheby's Hong Kong presents two extraordinary survivors from the same iconic vintage. One is the earliest known bottling of the famous Cask #5627. The other, Cask #4123, remains one of the greatest mysteries in Karuizawa collecting, with only two known hand-bottled examples. Together, they reveal a fascinating and little-known chapter in the history of Japan's most celebrated lost distillery.

entry.title: How Cézanne's Arlequin Set the Stage for Modernism | Sotheby's

media:group.media:title: How Cézanne's Arlequin Set the Stage for Modernism | Sotheby's
media:group.media:description:
Cézanne made just four harlequin paintings in his career, and this fall, the only one remaining in private hands is coming to Sotheby’s New York. ‘Arlequin,’ made between 1888 and 1890, sets the scene for the birth of modernity.
Here, Sotheby’s Helena Newman examines the elements of this harlequin that make it such a masterpiece of Cézanne’s career.
The subject, modeled on his son, stands unwaveringly with an almost mask-like expression on his face. This is in contrast to the energetic, opulent blue and red background, highlighting Cézanne’s innovative ability to build depth through manipulation of color and form.
This is a work of juxtaposition and immediacy. You see a solitary figure from the Commedia dell’arte, his defined, diamond costume is set against the lush, loosely painted environment—every element coming together to establish Cézanne as the 'father of modernism.'
Arlequin will be offered in Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection Evening Auction at Sotheby's New York on 18 November 2026.

entry.title: Why Does This 1000-Year-Old Chinese Vase Feel So Modern? | Sotheby's

media:group.media:title: Why Does This 1000-Year-Old Chinese Vase Feel So Modern? | Sotheby's
media:group.media:description:
A thousand years after it was made, this remarkable Cizhou vase still feels astonishingly alive. Its sweeping peony blooms, carved with confidence and spontaneity, capture a moment when ceramics were created not for emperors, but for a cultivated scholarly elite who prized elegance, restraint, and individuality. Every incision in the surface preserves the movement of a maker's hand across a millennium.
What makes this vessel so compelling is not only its rarity, but its immediacy. Formed during the Song Dynasty and decorated using the demanding sgraffiato technique, the vase bridges past and present with remarkable ease. The same generous silhouette that once graced literati gatherings feels perfectly at home in a contemporary interior, a reminder that great design rarely belongs to a single era.

entry.title: How to look at Joan Mitchell’s The Green Book of Barbara Guest | Sotheby’s

media:group.media:title: How to look at Joan Mitchell’s The Green Book of Barbara Guest | Sotheby’s
media:group.media:description:
Here is how to look at an abstract canvas by Joan Mitchell.
While it may look like one spontaneous burst of vibrant paint, ‘Green Book of Barbara Guest’ is filled with Mitchell’s careful decisions. Here, Sotheby’s Courtney Kremers connects this monumental composition to music or poetry. There is a rhythm to the way the paint moves across the canvas, and as your eyes follow along, you realize that not everything you see needs an explanation. It’s an energetic painting that celebrates the experience of looking.
Joan Mitchell’s ‘Green Book of Barbara Guest’ will be on offer as part of Sotheby's Contemporary Evening Auction, presented by CELINE, live in New York on 16 November at the historic Breuer building.

entry.title: Could This Be the First Patek Philippe 3970 Ever Made? | Sotheby’s

media:group.media:title: Could This Be the First Patek Philippe 3970 Ever Made? | Sotheby’s
media:group.media:description:
Collectors spend a lifetime searching for origins. The first edition, the earliest example, the moment a story begins. Few watches embody that pursuit quite like this Patek Philippe Reference 3970, a perpetual calendar chronograph that helped define an era of modern collecting and remains one of the most admired complicated watches ever produced.
Made in 1986, this remarkable example is believed to be the first numbered 3970, earning its nickname: "The First 3970." From its distinctive two-tone dial and feuille hands to its snap-on caseback and legendary Lemania-based calibre 27-70 Q movement, every detail points toward the earliest chapter of an icon's history. Four decades after its introduction, this watch feels less like a timepiece and more like a time capsule, preserving the moment one of Patek Philippe's most celebrated references first entered the world.

entry.title: Why Does This Rolex Belong in a Pilot’s Cockpit? | Sotheby’s

media:group.media:title: Why Does This Rolex Belong in a Pilot’s Cockpit? | Sotheby’s
media:group.media:description:
What kind of watch does a pilot wear when pushing an aircraft to its limits? For Ettore Wengi, one of Italy’s celebrated test pilots, the answer was a pink gold Rolex reference 6032. A member of the legendary “Squadriglia Folle”, or Mad Squadron, Wengi belonged to a generation for whom the sky was an invitation to go further. His Rolex was more than a beautiful object: it was a companion to a life spent testing the boundaries of flight.
On the back of the watch is a date that connects it to a remarkable moment in aviation history: 7 May 1959, the maiden flight of the Procaer F.15 Picchio, designed by Stelio Frati. Decades later, this exceptionally rare vintage Rolex chronograph returns to the airfield, where its story began. With only four pink gold examples known to have appeared on the market, it is a timepiece that brings together the worlds of horology, aviation and Italian design in a way few watches can.
